title: Compute Bottlenecks: Why Software-Only Explosions Stall

questions.question: In the two-factor view of AI progress, what does a 'software-only intelligence explosion' assume?
options: Physical compute and software efficiency both grow, but software grows faster than hardware
Software efficiency is frozen while physical compute keeps growing at the historical trend
Physical compute is held fixed and all further gains come from software efficiency improvements
Both factors are fixed and progress comes only from deploying more copies of the same model
questions.explanation: Effective compute = physical compute x software efficiency. The Forethought and AI 2027 software-only models deliberately freeze the hardware factor and ask whether software alone can compound.

questions.question: A research cycle spends 60% of wall-clock in labour stages and 40% waiting on experiment compute. With compute fixed, what is the maximum speedup from automating labour by any factor k?
options: 2.5x, because speedup = 1 / (0.60 / k + 0.40) tends to 1 / 0.40 as k grows
k times, because every stage of the pipeline is sped up by the same factor k
1.67x, because the labour share 0.60 is the part that limits the total speedup
No limit, because enough agent copies can run arbitrarily many experiments at once
questions.explanation: Amdahl's law: the un-accelerated stage's share bounds the speedup at 1 / f_compute = 2.5x. At k = 30 the pipeline is already at 2.38x, 95% of that ceiling.

questions.question: AI 2027 defines a Superhuman Coder as 30x as many agents as human engineers, each 30x faster. Why does the lesson's queue model NOT give a 900x research speedup?
options: Because the agents must each write their own evaluation code, which adds overhead per copy
Because more copies raise ideation quality only, which is not where the pipeline spends time
Because faster copies also make more mistakes, so most of their experiments must be re-run
Because every copy's experiments compete for the same GPU pool, whose throughput caps completions
questions.explanation: Copies parallelise thinking, but experiments need GPUs. Once N exceeds the knee (ceiling x single-agent cycle time), extra agents only lengthen the queue and each copy's cycle time.

questions.question: Anthropic's RSP v3.1 (April 2026) clarified the AI R&D threshold's 'doubling the rate of progress'. What does the threshold refer to?
options: Doubling the productivity of individual Anthropic researchers, measured by internal surveys
Doubling aggregate AI capability progress, i.e. compressing two years of 2018-2024 progress into one
Doubling the training compute of the frontier model within one calendar year of its release
Doubling the number of experiments per week that the internal research cluster can complete
questions.explanation: v3.1 says 'we mean the former and not the latter': aggregate capability progress, not researcher productivity. The 2018-2024 yardstick includes the compute growth of those years, so it is not a software-only bar.

questions.question: Running experiments at small scale lowers the compute fraction of a cycle (e.g. 0.40 to 0.20). What does this do to a software-only explosion, and what is the catch?
options: It removes the ceiling entirely, since small experiments need no shared GPU pool at all
It lowers the ceiling from 2.5x to 1.67x, because labour now dominates the cycle time
It raises the ceiling from 2.5x to 5x, but results must extrapolate to frontier scale to count
It leaves the ceiling at 2.5x unchanged, because the compute stage is still present in the cycle
questions.explanation: The ceiling is 1 / f_compute, so halving f_compute doubles it. The escape only works if small-scale findings transfer to large scale; that extrapolation risk is not something more agent copies can remove.

questions.question: Why does the lesson call the compute bottleneck a 'safety handle' and not only a limit on progress?
options: Compute is observable and accountable (chips, power, training runs), while software gains are not
Compute can be throttled instantly by any lab that notices a dangerous capability emerging
Compute growth is the only input that AI agents cannot influence through their own research
Compute shortages force labs to publish their algorithms, which lets regulators inspect them
questions.explanation: A software-only loop would be nearly invisible to outsiders; a loop that needs compute leaves a trail that export controls and compute accounting can govern. Lesson 21 builds on this.
